name: Bloom filters
hook: The bouncer with a bad memory. Add words, light bulbs, and catch the bouncer waving in a stranger.
pageTitle: Bloom filters, explained with light bulbs
title: The bouncer with a bad memory
subtitle: A hands-on tour of Bloom filters, in four short steps.

paras: Your browser wants to warn you before you open a dodgy website. There are millions of them, and the list changes every day.

Downloading the whole list to your phone is too heavy. So early versions of Chrome kept a tiny, blurry sketch of the list instead. The sketch can never say "yes, definitely". It can only say "definitely not" or "hmm, probably".
That blurry sketch is a Bloom filter. It's like a bouncer who forgets faces but remembers a few odd details: "green jacket, tall, laughs loudly". Anyone matching all three gets a second look.
This strip of bulbs is all the memory the bouncer gets. Type a word and hit Add. The word gets scrambled three different ways, and each scramble points at one bulb. Those bulbs turn on.
Then Check a word. If any of its three bulbs is dark, the bouncer is certain: never seen it. If all three glow, it's a "probably".
Here's the catch. Bulbs never turn off, and different words can share bulbs. Fill the strip with strangers, then check a word you never added. Watch the bouncer wave it through anyway.
Play with the sliders: more bulbs means fewer mistakes, and more scrambles per word helps too, until the strip gets crowded.

origin.intro: It's 1970. Burton H. Bloom, a programmer at Computer Usage Company in Massachusetts, publishes a five-page paper in Communications of the ACM: "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors".

timeline.label: The problem
timeline.text: Computers had tiny fast memory (core) and big slow storage (disk). Bloom's example was a program that adds hyphens to words. About 90% of words follow simple rules. The awkward 50,000 or so need a dictionary lookup, and the dictionary only fits on disk.

timeline.label: The naive fix
timeline.text: Look every word up on disk. Slow, because most trips to the disk come back empty-handed.

timeline.label: The insight
timeline.text: Keep a blurry sketch of the awkward words in fast memory. A "definitely not" skips the disk. A "probably" pays for one disk trip, and the occasional false alarm just costs a wasted trip, not a wrong hyphen. Bloom worked out this cut disk visits by about 84%.

timeline.label: Since then
timeline.text: The idea sat quietly for decades, then took off in the 1990s and 2000s when web caches, databases and networks all hit the same wall: too much data, too little fast memory. Cousins appeared too: counting Bloom filters (which can delete), cuckoo filters, and learned filters that use a small model as the first pass.

origin.takeaway: Notice what Bloom actually traded: he gave up a little correctness to gain a lot of memory. That trade is the whole trick, and it's why the strip above breaks the way it does.

uses.intro: That "definitely not" answer is the whole point. It lets a system skip expensive work with total confidence, and only pay the full price on a "probably".

items.title: Browsers and URL checks
items.text: Is this site on the danger list? A dark bulb means "no, carry on" with no network call at all.

items.title: Databases like Cassandra and RocksDB
items.text: Is this key inside this file on disk? Each file can keep a Bloom filter so the database skips files that definitely don't have it.

items.title: Caches and CDNs
items.text: Has anyone asked for this item before? Only cache it the second time, so one-hit wonders don't clog the shelf.

uses.caveat: What it can't do: it never says a definite yes, and you can't remove a word once added, because turning off a bulb might erase someone else's clue.
